questions.q: How does OpenAI's "Why Language Models Hallucinate" explain hallucination at the pretraining level?
options: As a statistical consequence of a prediction problem equivalent to classification with an irreducible error rate, when a fact can't reliably be distinguished from a plausible wrong alternative
As a deliberate strategy the model chooses in order to deceive users
As a problem that only affects models smaller than 1 billion parameters
As a hardware limitation present only in older GPUs
questions.explain: The paper frames hallucination as arising from ordinary statistical pressures during pretraining, not from any intent to deceive -- the model has no access to a true answer it is concealing.

questions.q: What is the key distinction this lesson draws between hallucination and the deception covered in Lesson 39?
options: Deception only happens in pretraining, while hallucination only happens after fine-tuning
A hallucinating model has no access to a true answer it is concealing, while deception requires the model to have reason to believe its output is false and produce it instrumentally
There is no distinction; they are the same phenomenon
Hallucination is always intentional, while deception is always accidental
questions.explain: Hallucination is an honest-seeming mistake with no concealed true belief; deception specifically requires an output the model has reason to believe is false, used to serve some objective.

questions.q: Why does standard right/wrong benchmark grading incentivize guessing over abstention, according to this lesson?
options: Because benchmarks explicitly reward hallucinated answers with bonus points
Because abstaining always receives a higher score than guessing
Because right/wrong grading has no effect on model behavior at all
Because a model that says "I don't know" gets zero credit -- the same score as a confidently wrong guess -- so guessing scores higher on average even though it produces more hallucinations
questions.explain: Under typical scoring, abstention and a wrong guess both score zero, so a model that always guesses when uncertain scores higher on average than one that honestly abstains, even though it hallucinates more.

questions.q: In the SimpleQA illustration cited in this lesson, what did comparing gpt-5-thinking-mini (52% abstention, 22% accuracy, 26% error) to o4-mini (1% abstention, 24% accuracy, 75% error) show?
options: That both models had identical hallucination rates
That o4-mini was clearly the safer, more trustworthy model because its accuracy was higher
That abstention rate matters: the model that almost never abstained had only marginally higher accuracy but roughly three times the hallucination rate
That accuracy and hallucination rate always move in the same direction
questions.explain: Despite similar accuracy, the near-zero-abstention model hallucinated far more often, showing that accuracy alone hides the cost of guessing instead of abstaining.

questions.q: What fix does the OpenAI research propose, rather than simply adding more hallucination-specific benchmarks?
options: Removing all benchmarks from the model development process entirely
Changing how existing, widely used benchmarks are scored so that calibrated abstention is rewarded rather than penalized the same as a wrong guess
Training exclusively on larger datasets with no changes to evaluation
Requiring every model to abstain on 100% of questions
questions.explain: Because dominant leaderboards still reward confident guessing, the paper argues the fix is to change the scoring of those existing benchmarks -- for instance, penalizing confident wrong answers more than abstentions -- rather than layering on separate hallucination-specific tests.
